The Questions Every Parent Should Ask Before Buying an E-Bike or E-Scooter

By
DMM Guest Blogger
-
July 31, 2026
0
Facebook
X
Pinterest
ReddIt
Email
    Listen to audio version of this article
    Sponsored by
    0:00 / 5:15
    Instaread

    I was stopped at a busy intersection earlier this week when I had one of those stomach-drop moments that only a parent knows.

    A girl who couldn’t have been more than 10 years old zipped past me on an electric scooter —no helmet in sight—riding alongside cars going about 40 miles per hour. 

    Thankfully, she made it across safely. But in the few seconds I watched her ride past, my mom-brain traveled to about a dozen worst case scenarios. My public health brain did the same!

    Working in communications for the Polk County Health Department, I know we’re seeing more children seriously injured while riding motorized bikes and scooters. Emergency departments across the country are reporting sharp increases in injuries, including traumatic brain injuries, broken bones, and internal injuries. The American Academy of Pediatrics has raised concerns as e-bike and e-scooter injuries continue to increase among children and teens.

    It’s easy to see why.

    Unlike the scooters and bikes many of us grew up with, today’s electric versions are heavier, accelerate quickly, and many reach speeds of 20 miles per hour or more. The faster a child is traveling, the less time they have to react and the more severe a crash can become.

    That’s also why it’s important for parents to know exactly what their child is riding. Not every electric ride is an e-scooter or e-bike. Some are actually mopeds, motorcycles, or dirt bikes that are capable of much higher speeds and subject to different rules. Understanding the difference—and knowing where each type of device is legal to ride in your community—is an important part of keeping kids safe.

    As parents, we spend countless hours helping our kids prepare for new milestones. We don’t hand over car keys without teaching the rules of the road. We don’t send them into a pool before they’re ready.

    Motorized bikes and scooters deserve that same level of thought.

    The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that children younger than 16 should not operate or ride on motorized or shared e-scooters. For e-bikes, the AAP encourages parents to carefully consider whether a child has the maturity, judgment and riding skills needed before allowing them to ride. They also recommend setting clear family rules before the first ride—not after something goes wrong.

    If you’re considering an e-bike or e-scooter for your child or teenager, here are a few questions worth asking first:

      • How fast does it go? Understand whether it’s an e-bike, an e-scooter, or a higher-powered device. They aren’t all the same, and some can travel much faster than others.
      • Is my child mature enough to consistently make safe decisions? Speed is exciting, but it also requires quick judgment.
      • Is this device legal where they’ll be riding? Make sure you know where it’s allowed to be ridden and whether there are age or helmet requirements.
      • Will they wear a properly fitted helmet that is rated for the speed they’re traveling during every single ride? Helmets save lives, and should be worn on every scooter or bike—even if powered solely by pedals.
      • Do they understand the rules of the road? Riding predictably, yielding to pedestrians and knowing how to navigate intersections all matter.
      • Can they ride without distractions? No phones. No earbuds. Their full attention should be on what’s around them.
      • Where will they be riding? Sidewalks, streets, trails and parks all come with different risks. Talk through those situations before they happen.

    As both a public health professional and a mom, I know these conversations with kids aren’t always easy. Especially when your child says, “But everyone else has one!” 

    Open conversations with your child can help you decide if they’re truly ready to ride an e-scooter or e-bike, and sometimes the safest answer is, “Not yet.”

    The goal isn’t to take the fun out of childhood. It’s to make sure childhood lasts.

    Every conversation about helmets, speed, local laws, and safe riding is an investment in your child’s future. They’re small decisions that can prevent life-changing injuries.

    At the Polk County Health Department, these conversations are part of our We All Arrive traffic safety initiative. Our goal is simple: no matter how you’re traveling—walking, biking, driving, rolling or riding—everyone deserves to make it home safely.

    Because no matter how your family gets from one place to another, the goal is always the same: We all arrive.

    Sources:

    • American Academy of Pediatrics. E-Scooters: What Parents Need to Know. 
    • American Academy of Pediatrics. Are Electric Bikes (E-Bikes) Safe for Children? 
    • National Electronic Injury Surveillance System (NEISS) data summarized by the American Academy of Pediatrics, showing increasing pediatric e-bike and e-scooter injuries treated in U.S. emergency departments.

    Addie Olson is a communications leader, former journalist, and public health professional who serves as Communications Supervisor for the Polk County Health Department. She is passionate about making complex health topics clear, relatable, and actionable so families can make informed decisions. Outside of work, she’s a mom to a curious 4-year-old who keeps her on her toes and reminds her every day why creating healthier, safer communities matters. Addie believes the best stories are the ones that help people feel informed, connected, and empowered.
